chapters.title: Chapter 3: Valuing a Business Against Its Peers

lessons.title: Choosing Comparable Companies and Transactions Using screener.in

children.text: The multiple is the easy part. The hard part, and the part that decides whether your number survives contact with a buyer, is choosing whose multiple to borrow. A peer set assembled in ten minutes from an industry label will give you an answer that is confidently wrong. This lesson is the workflow for doing it properly, using tools any Indian manager can open right now.

body.text: A comparable company is not one that sells similar products. It is one that would face the same questions from an investor: same growth, same margins, same capital intensity, same customers, same risks. Similar products are where you start looking, not where you stop.

children.text: Two Kinds of Comparables

cells: Multiples at which listed peers trade today
Multiples paid in actual acquisitions of similar businesses
The price of a small minority stake, priced daily by the market
The price of control, usually including a premium and the buyer's synergies
Where to find them in India
screener.in, NSE and BSE websites, company results
Deal announcements, letters of offer, scheme documents, subscription databases
Valuing a minority stake, or a sanity check on any valuation
Valuing a controlling stake in a sale process

body.text: Quoting a transaction multiple to value a 10% minority stake overstates the value, because the buyer in that deal paid for control and for synergies the minority investor will never enjoy. Quoting a trading multiple to price a 100% sale understates it for the same reason in reverse. Match the multiple to the stake being valued.

children.text: What "Comparable" Actually Requires
Run every candidate peer through the same seven tests. A company that fails three of them is not a peer, however familiar the brand.

cells: A branded manufacturer and a contract manufacturer are different businesses even with identical products
A ₹200 crore revenue company does not deserve a ₹20,000 crore company's multiple
The single biggest driver of differences in multiples
Three and five year sales growth
Two companies at the same revenue with different margins are different businesses
Asset heavy businesses need more investment for the same growth
Fixed assets to sales, and return on capital employed
A regional player with one state's distribution is not a national brand
Segment disclosures and the management discussion
Consolidated against standalone, and differences in lease treatment, distort every ratio
Consolidated financial statements, and the notes

children.text: The screener.in Workflow, Step by Step
Take a fictional target: Marathwada Namkeen Private Limited, a regional packaged snacks company in Maharashtra with revenue of ₹300 crore and EBITDA of ₹45 crore. Here is how to build its peer set.
Start from a known listed peer.

Open screener.in and search a listed company in the same business. For packaged snacks in India that means names such as Bikaji Foods International, Gopal Snacks and Prataap Snacks, all listed on the NSE.
Open the Peers section.

Screener generates a peer list from the industry classification. Treat it as a starting list, not an answer: industry codes routinely put a ₹60,000 crore diversified giant next to a single-category regional player.
Switch to consolidated.
Use the consolidated view for every company in the set, or the ratios will not be comparable.
Record the same fields for each peer.
Market capitalisation, revenue, three year sales growth, operating margin, return on capital employed, P/E, and borrowings and cash so you can compute enterprise value yourself.
Cut the list by the seven tests.
Drop the giants, the conglomerates and anyone whose business model differs. You are aiming for four to eight genuine peers, not twenty names.
Take the median, and look at the range.
Then adjust deliberately for how your target differs from that median.

body.label: Screener.in: Bikaji Foods International
body.description: Open the Peers section and try the workflow above on a live peer set. Pull today's figures rather than relying on any number printed in a course, because multiples change every trading day.

children.text: Median, Not Average

Suppose the screen throws up five genuine peers trading at these EV/EBITDA multiples: 9, 11, 14, 18 and 35 times. The 35 belongs to a company that just announced a large acquisition and has depressed current earnings.

stats.label: Range
stats.context: Which is itself the most honest finding

body.text: The gap between 14 and 17.4 is ₹153 crore of value on ₹45 crore of EBITDA. One outlier, silently included in an average, moves the answer by more than most negotiations do. Use the median, disclose the range, and say in one line why any peer was excluded.

body.title: Find the median
body.prompt: After cutting your list you are left with four genuine peers, trading at EV/EBITDA multiples of 12, 15, 16 and 19 times. What is the median multiple?
body.explanation: With an even number of peers the median is the average of the two middle values: (15 + 16) ÷ 2 = 15.5 times. With four peers you should also show the range, because a single peer carries a quarter of the weight.

children.text: Adjusting the Median to Your Company

The median describes the peers, not your target. Marathwada Namkeen is smaller, unlisted, regional and dependent on one promoter. Each of those differences moves the multiple, and each adjustment must be written down and justified.

body.caption: From the peer median to a value for the target

cells: Adjust for smaller size, regional presence and lack of marketability
₹80 crore of borrowings, no surplus cash

body.text: The 25% in that table is where an honest valuation and a convenient one part company. A discount of that size needs reasoning: how much smaller, how concentrated the distribution, how dependent on the promoter, how illiquid the shares. "Standard practice" is not a reason, and a buyer's adviser will test it line by line.

body.title: Pick the better comparable
body.question: You are valuing Marathwada Namkeen, a ₹300 crore revenue regional snacks maker growing 12% a year. Two candidate peers: a ₹60,000 crore national FMCG conglomerate trading at 55 times earnings, and a ₹3,000 crore single-category regional snacks company growing 14% a year and trading at 22 times earnings. Which is the better comparable, and why?
options: The conglomerate, because it is the market leader and sets the benchmark for the sector
The regional snacks company, because its size, category focus and growth rate are far closer to the target
Neither, since only unlisted companies can be compared with an unlisted target
Both should be averaged, to balance the two extremes
body.explanation: The conglomerate has diversified categories, national distribution, a huge balance sheet and a completely different risk profile, and its 55 times multiple reflects all of that. The regional player shares the category, the growth rate and roughly the scale of ambition. Averaging the two is the worst option: it produces a number neither company would recognise and that nobody can defend.

children.text: Where Indian Deal Multiples Hide

Transaction comparables are harder to find than trading comparables, because private deals do not publish their EBITDA. Most of the useful information sits in documents that are public but rarely read.
Company announcements and investor presentations for listed acquirers, which often disclose the enterprise value and sometimes the multiple paid
Letters of offer for open offers under the SEBI takeover code, which set out the valuation basis in detail
Scheme of arrangement documents filed with the exchanges for mergers and demergers, which attach the valuer's report and the share exchange ratio
Annual reports of the acquirer, where the purchase price allocation note shows what was paid and what it was allocated to
Subscription databases such as Venture Intelligence or VCCEdge, where budget allows
Financial statements of unlisted targets filed with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, which let you compute the multiple yourself once the price is public

Two transactions from earlier in this course show what is usually available: Hindustan Unilever's acquisition of Minimalist at a valuation of ₹2,955 crore against FY24 revenue of about ₹347 crore, and Tata Consumer Products' acquisition of Capital Foods at an enterprise value of ₹5,100 crore. The first gives you a revenue multiple directly. The second gives you a price, and you would need the target's filed financials to turn it into a multiple.

body.title: Two peer sets, two different answers

columns.label: A peer set built to flatter
points: Twenty names taken straight from the industry classification
Includes the fastest growing company in the sector as an "aspirational" peer
Uses the mean, not the median
Mixes trailing multiples for some peers and forward for others
No adjustment for the target being unlisted and smaller

columns.label: A peer set that survives diligence
points: Five to eight names, each justified in a sentence
Exclusions listed with reasons, so the reader can disagree with the logic
Median presented with the full range around it
Same basis for every peer: consolidated, same financial year, same trailing or forward choice
Explicit, evidenced adjustments for size, liquidity and concentration

body.title: The banker's comp set
body.scenario: You are the CFO of Marathwada Namkeen. The investment bank running your fundraise circulates a valuation note using a peer set of three listed FMCG companies, all with national distribution and revenue above ₹10,000 crore, trading at a mean EV/EBITDA of 32 times. On that basis they value your business at ₹1,440 crore. The promoter is delighted. The term sheets that arrive two months later are all between ₹450 crore and ₹550 crore.
body.prompt: What went wrong, and what would you have asked for upfront?
body.modelAnswer:
What went wrong:
1. The peers are not comparable. National FMCG companies with 30 times our revenue, diversified categories and decades-old brands carry multiples that reflect exactly those advantages.
2. A mean of three companies is not a peer set. Three observations, averaged rather than taken at the median, with no range disclosed.
3. No adjustment was made for size, for being unlisted, for regional concentration or for promoter dependence.
4. The expectation set inside the company is now the real damage. Every genuine offer looks like an insult against ₹1,440 crore, and the promoter may reject a fair price out of anchoring.

What I would have asked for upfront:
1. A peer set of at least five companies closer to our size and category, with each inclusion and exclusion justified in one line.
2. The median and the full range, not the mean.
3. Both a trading comparables view and a transaction comparables view, with the difference between them explained as the control premium.
4. A cross-check by a second method, such as a DCF, so the answer does not rest entirely on borrowed multiples.
5. A stated basis: consolidated figures, the same financial year for every peer, and trailing or forward applied consistently.
6. A range presented to the board, with the assumptions written down, rather than a single headline number.

body.title: Which statistic
body.textWithBlank: When summarising a peer set, use the ___ rather than the mean, because a single outlier can drag an average far away from the typical peer.
body.explanation: In the lesson's example the median was 14 times and the mean 17.4 times, a difference worth ₹153 crore on ₹45 crore of EBITDA.

body.title: Build a defensible peer set
steps: Write down the business model of your target in two sentences before looking at any peer
Start from the industry list, then cut it by size, growth, margins and capital intensity
Keep four to eight peers, and record one line of reasoning for every inclusion and exclusion
Use consolidated figures, the same financial year and the same trailing or forward basis throughout
Compute enterprise value yourself from market capitalisation, borrowings and cash
Report the median with the range, never the mean alone
Separate trading comparables from transaction comparables, and match them to the stake being valued
State every adjustment, its size and the evidence for it
Cross-check the answer against a second valuation method before circulating it

cards.definition: Multiples at which listed peers trade today, reflecting minority stakes.
Multiples paid in actual acquisitions, reflecting control and often synergies.
The curated group of companies whose multiples you borrow, each justified.
The middle value in a sorted set, the right summary statistic for a small peer group.
The extra paid to acquire control, which is why transaction multiples exceed trading multiples.
A deliberate reduction applied when the target is materially smaller than its listed peers.
The note in an acquirer's annual report showing what was paid and how it was allocated across assets and goodwill.

points: Comparable means comparable in economics, not in product. Test every candidate on business model, size, growth, margins, capital intensity, geography and accounting basis.
Trading comparables price minority stakes. Transaction comparables price control. Match the type to the stake you are valuing.
The screener.in peer list is generated from industry codes and always needs manual curation down to four to eight real peers.
Use the median and disclose the range. In this lesson's set the median was 14 times against a mean of 17.4 times.
Applying 14 times to ₹45 crore of EBITDA gave ₹630 crore, and only after a documented 25% adjustment and ₹80 crore of net debt did it become ₹392.5 crore of equity value.
Indian deal multiples can be reconstructed from letters of offer, scheme documents, purchase price allocation notes and MCA filings.
An inflated peer set does its worst damage inside your own company, by anchoring the board on a number no buyer will pay.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Marathwada Namkeen is fictional, and every multiple used in the worked examples is illustrative. The listed companies named are examples of where to begin a search, not recommendations, and their actual multiples change every trading day. Always pull current figures before using them in live work.
